analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicare preventive, mental health, and low-income benefits while restricting aggressive sales practices by private Medicare plans.
analysis.headline: The Senate blocked the bill from reaching a floor vote on June 12, 2008, when a procedural vote to open debate failed 54-39, with 38 of 49 Republicans voting no.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would expand Medicare in several ways: cover more preventive services with no deductible, gradually eliminate the extra 50% copay seniors pay for outpatient mental health care, extend programs that help low-income beneficiaries afford premiums and drugs, and boost payments to doctors and rural hospitals. It would also bar Medicare Advantage insurers and drug plans from door-to-door selling, unsolicited telemarketing, and cross-selling annuities or life insurance to seniors, and would strip one private accreditor of its special status in hospital certification. The bill never reached the Senate floor: a vote to open debate got 54 of the 60 needed.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — especially seniors needing mental health care, preventive screenings, and low-income beneficiaries — plus rural hospitals, ambulance services, and physicians who would have gotten payment increases instead of a scheduled cut.

how_it_helps.text: Gradually eliminates the discriminatory 50% copayment Medicare charges for outpatient psychiatric care, reaching full parity by 2014, and adjusts Part B to help pay for it.

Adds coverage of preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, waives the deductible for the initial wellness exam, and extends the enrollment window for that exam from six months to a year.

Extends the Qualifying Individual program (which pays Medicare premiums for low-income seniors) through December 2009 with roughly $600 million in additional funding, waives Part D late-enrollment penalties for subsidy-eligible people, and exempts life insurance value when determining low-income subsidy eligibility.
Sets a 1.1% physician payment update for 2009 instead of the scheduled cut, adds incentives for electronic prescribing, and extends quality-reporting bonus payments.

Bars Medicare Advantage plans and drug plans from door-to-door solicitation, outbound telemarketing, cross-selling non-health products like annuities, providing meals at sales events, and marketing in health care settings, and lets states investigate agents and brokers.

Helps rural areas: grants for mental health services to rural veterans, rebasing for sole community hospitals, extended rural ambulance payments, a rural pharmacy and community health demonstration, and $55 million a year for the rural hospital flexibility program.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the Medicare trust funds finance the benefit expansions and provider payments; Medicare Advantage insurers, their agents and brokers, and the Joint Commission accreditor bear new restrictions and lost privileges.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare trust funds and private plan insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill adds substantial federal spending — new preventive and low-income benefits, roughly $600 million for the QI program, grants for outreach and rural hospitals, and the 1.1% physician update — drawing on the Medicare trust funds at a time when their long-term finances were already strained.

The physician payment fix is temporary: the 1.1% update applies only to 2009, and the law would compute 2010 payments as if the increase never happened, deferring the underlying payment formula problem rather than solving it.

Some provisions are targeted provider givebacks — such as letting sole community hospitals recompute their payment rates upward — that add cost for taxpayers without a corresponding benefit to patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a real gain for seniors: mental health parity in Medicare copays, new preventive coverage, and stronger help for low-income beneficiaries, paid for partly through offsets like imaging and wheelchair payment changes and restrictions on private-plan marketing. The main honest objection is cost: it layers new spending onto a program with long-term financing gaps, and its physician payment fix only postpones the larger problem by a year.

outcome.mechanism: Republican senators refused to let the bill even come up for debate — a cloture vote to proceed failed 54-39 when 60 votes were needed — so the bill died on the Senate calendar without ever getting an up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus introduced the bill on June 6, 2008, joined by Sens. Snowe, Rockefeller, and Smith, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The bill was placed on the Senate calendar on June 9, and a motion to proceed to it — the step needed to begin debate — was made and a cloture motion filed on June 10.
On June 12, 2008, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 54-39; invoking cloture required 60 votes, so the Senate never opened debate on the bill.
The vote split sharply by party: 43 of 49 Democrats voted to proceed while 38 of 49 Republicans voted no; only 9 Republicans supported moving forward.
After the failed vote, the motion to proceed was withdrawn, leaving the bill on the calendar with no floor vote for the remainder of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers and their agents and brokers avoided the new marketing restrictions, and the Joint Commission kept its exclusive hospital accreditation role; seniors did not get the mental health parity and low-income benefits this bill would have provided through this vehicle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private Medicare plans and their agents

sides.party_line_note: The cloture vote split by party: 43 of 49 Democrats voted yes and 38 of 49 Republicans voted no, with only 9 Republicans crossing over; the 54-39 result fell short of the 60 votes needed.

industries.note: The bill bans door-to-door solicitation, unsolicited telemarketing, cross-selling annuities and life insurance, and meals at sales events, and tightens rules on private-fee-for-service plans and agent compensation. Their gain under the old rules came from high-pressure enrollment tactics that often left seniors in plans that did not fit their needs.
Agents would face state licensing and appointment requirements, mandatory training and testing, and compensation guidelines designed to stop paying them to steer seniors into inappropriate plans.

A 1.1% payment update for 2009 instead of a scheduled cut, e-prescribing incentives, and extended quality bonuses. Keeping physician payments stable protects seniors' access to doctors who might otherwise stop taking Medicare patients.
The bill revokes the Joint Commission's unique authority to deem hospitals compliant with Medicare standards, forcing it to compete for recognition with other accreditors under Secretary review.

Rebasing for sole community hospitals, extended rural ambulance payments, rural hospital flexibility grants, and a community health demonstration would channel more federal payment into rural facilities that serve seniors and veterans with few alternatives.

Insurers would have to offer a range of standardized supplemental policies and implement updated NAIC standards, expanding choices for beneficiaries while conforming their products to new benefit designs.
